## Resolution

Audit basis: the six completed investigations, all against current `origin/main` at [`f2e7af0`](https://github.com/chrisdoc/hevy-mcp/commit/f2e7af0ee3a02b6a0c6fa7820895db3882b7be4c):

- [Map change-amplification and duplication hotspots](https://github.com/chrisdoc/hevy-mcp/issues/864#issuecomment-5165193087)
- [Audit failure containment and recovery across runtimes](https://github.com/chrisdoc/hevy-mcp/issues/859#issuecomment-5165304979)
- [Audit operator journeys from installation through diagnosis](https://github.com/chrisdoc/hevy-mcp/issues/861#issuecomment-5165380704)
- [Audit MCP tool contracts for AI-client usability](https://github.com/chrisdoc/hevy-mcp/issues/862#issuecomment-5165470475)
- [Audit test, generation, CI, and release safety nets](https://github.com/chrisdoc/hevy-mcp/issues/860#issuecomment-5165880199)
- [Benchmark hevy-mcp against current MCP and SDK guidance](https://github.com/chrisdoc/hevy-mcp/issues/863#issuecomment-5166014979)

### Synthesis decision

The audits do **not** imply six independent programs. They repeatedly found the same missing ownership at four levels:

1. domain operations and capability semantics;
2. invocation control, outcomes, and safe recovery;
3. product/repository metadata and its projections; and
4. adapter-specific lifecycle behavior.

The preferred architecture is a new runtime-neutral **Hevy operations module** between the generated client and both user adapters, supported by a small execution/outcome interface and consumed through thin MCP and CLI adapters. Separately, three linked declarative models should drive product, repository, and validation projections. This is deliberately **not one universal manifest**: each model owns a distinct vocabulary and references the others by stable identifiers.

The resulting dependency shape is:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    HC[Hevy client adapter] --> OP[Hevy operations module]
    EO[Execution and outcome model] --> HC
    EO --> OP
    OP --> MCP[MCP capability adapter]
    OP --> CLI[CLI adapter]
    MCP --> PS[Protocol serving module]
    PS --> NODE[Node runtime adapter]
    PS --> WORKER[Worker runtime adapter]

    CAP[Capability model] --> OP
    CAP --> MCP
    CAP --> CLI
    CAP --> TEST[Validation and evaluation]
    PRODUCT[Operator/product model] --> NODE
    PRODUCT --> WORKER
    PRODUCT --> CLI
    PRODUCT --> DOCS[Generated operator projections]
    TOPO[Repository topology model] --> TEST
    LANE[Validation-lane manifest] --> TEST
```

Arrows show consumption, not a requirement to create a package for every box.

## Ownership map

| Module / seam | Owns | Must not own |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Hevy client adapter** | Generated/native-fetch mechanics, authentication header, attempt timeout, abortable request/body handling, upstream response decoding, dispatch/response phase facts | MCP/CLI presentation, task intent, mutation confirmation, pagination workflows, user recovery prose |
| **Hevy operations module** | Shared read/write intents, normalization, expected absence, pagination, search, composite workflows, approved cache/degradation policy, mutation semantics, canonical field metadata | MCP transport, CLI parsing/rendering, Node/Worker lifecycle, generated-client internals |
| **Execution and outcome model** | Cancellation, absolute deadline, operation safety, request phase, commit state, stable safe failure taxonomy, retry/recovery fields, privacy-safe facts | Adapter-specific text, HTTP/MCP status projection, telemetry exporter implementation |
| **Capability model** | Stable capability IDs, selection intent, input/output semantics, field mappings, write behavior, safety annotations, success/outcome contracts | CI lane membership, package topology, deployment credentials, hand-written tutorials |
| **MCP capability adapter** | Projection of capabilities into tools, prompts, resources, structured/text responses, MCP-only presentation metadata | Duplicate Hevy orchestration or its own failure taxonomy |
| **Protocol serving module** | One primitive registry served through 2025 and 2026 protocol eras, modern discovery/metadata, legacy compatibility, logging quarantine | Collapsing Node stateful HTTP and Worker stateless transport implementations |
| **CLI adapter** | Command-local declaration/parsing, TTY confirmation and dry-run presentation, shell output/exit-code projection | Reimplementing operation catalog, pagination, recovery policy, or field semantics |
| **Operator experience module** | Product/surface catalog, config/auth/readiness lifecycle, diagnostic checks, version/upgrade/recovery actions, human and JSON projections | Capability implementation, repository package graph, generic prose as source of truth |
| **Repository control-plane module** | Workspace topology, allowed dependencies, exports, publishability, bundle/release propagation, artifact provenance, validation-lane registry | Runtime operation behavior, secrets, duplicating workflow implementations as data |
| **Validation and evaluation module** | Generation closure, contract matrix, official conformance, task evaluation, coverage denominator, candidate-artifact/release gates, measured feedback | Redefining capability/product/topology semantics that its tests consume |

This placement passes the deletion test:

- deleting the Hevy operations module would redistribute policy across MCP and CLI;
- deleting the execution/outcome model would redistribute cancellation, retry, safe diagnostics, and recovery across every adapter;
- deleting the declarative models would restore separate registries in code, prose, tests, and workflows;
- deleting an adapter leaves its surface-specific behavior behind, but does not erase shared domain policy.

## Deduplicated opportunity set advancing to portfolio selection

### 1. Establish end-to-end invocation control and outcomes

This consolidates cancellation/deadlines, retry budgets, phase-aware errors, ambiguous writes, safe failure facts, structured mutation results, telemetry classification, and operator recovery.

The interface should carry a caller signal, one absolute deadline, operation safety, and progress/reporting hooks. The Hevy client should accept low-level request control on every operation and emit transport phase facts; the operations module should turn those into stable domain outcomes; MCP, CLI, HTTP, and telemetry should only project them.

Acceptance must prove abortability across fetch, body consumption, backoff, pagination, composite workflows, disconnect, eviction, SIGINT, and shutdown; it must also prove that non-idempotent writes are not automatically retried and unknown commit state remains explicit.

### 2. Create the shared Hevy operations and capability module

The strongest maintainer-leverage seam is a new runtime-neutral workspace—provisionally `@hevy-mcp/operations`—in the dependency graph:

`hevy-client → operations → core → node/worker`, with `operations → cli`.

It should expose intent-level operations and their typed descriptors while hiding generated-client calls, normalization, pagination, expected absence, mutation replacement/patch rules, canonical field spelling, and composite workflows. MCP and CLI are the two real production adapters; an in-memory Hevy port is the test adapter.

This absorbs the duplicated CLI/MCP operation catalog, partial core policy seams, pagination response repetition, body-measurement field ownership, mutation semantics, and cross-tool field mapping. It does not merge MCP schemas with generated Hevy schemas.

### 3. Project MCP and CLI contracts instead of hand-reconstructing them

The capability model should generate or validate:

- MCP input/output schemas, annotations, structured mutation results, text compatibility, prompts/resources, titles/icons/completion metadata, and field mappings;
- CLI route metadata, schema/examples/templates, JSON success/error envelopes, dry-run/replacement summaries, and command help; and
- documentation and contract/evaluation fixtures.

CLI command modules remain local and domain-named because parsing and human presentation genuinely vary. MCP tools remain explicit capabilities rather than a generic stringly dispatcher. The shared descriptor removes duplicated knowledge without flattening either adapter.

### 4. Introduce one dual-era protocol-serving seam

One MCP primitive factory should serve both the 2025 interoperability floor and the 2026 opt-in protocol through SDK-supported adapters. It should own `server/discover`, per-request metadata, standard headers, cache hints, and legacy logging quarantine.

Node stdio, Node HTTP, and Worker HTTP remain separate adapters. Stateful Node session behavior stays isolated as legacy/runtime policy; Worker stateless request isolation stays intact. A modern-only cutover is not accepted without client and conformance evidence.

### 5. Build an executable operator experience contract

A structured product model should own surfaces, versions, Node requirements, auth modes, canonical endpoints, configuration schema/precedence, readiness states, diagnostics, upgrade/rollback, and recovery actions.

A deep doctor/preflight module should return versioned facts through human and JSON adapters, with ports for runtime, DNS/network, API auth, transport policy, OAuth metadata, and Worker bindings. README tables, package docs, deployment runbooks, migration indexes, and support bundles should be projections or validated examples, while hand-written prose retains rationale.

This consolidates operator diagnostics, safe failure facts, config normalization, hosted naming, readiness/version surfaces, deployment verification, and recovery guidance without making documentation a second registry.

### 6. Replace repository check duplication with linked control-plane models

Use separate but linked owners for:

- **topology:** workspaces, dependency rules, exports, publishability, bundles, release propagation;
- **artifact provenance:** spec normalization, generated destination, public barrels, manifests, packages/containers/Worker candidates; and
- **validation lanes:** selector, runtime, credentials, artifacts, gate class, comparison semantics, and change-impact routing.

Local hooks, pull requests, release workflows, documentation, and drift jobs should consume these models. Runtime-diverse Vitest configurations and external GitHub/Cloudflare adapters remain separate.

The generated-client output defect is an independently actionable prerequisite: generation must target the tracked package tree, never recreate root `src/`, and a hermetic regenerate-and-clean-diff gate must prove closure before later safety-net work.

### 7. Generate enforcement and evidence from accepted models

The validation/evaluation layer should consume, not redefine, the capability, product, topology, and lane models. It owns:

- complete tool/prompt/resource contract matrices;
- deterministic AI-client task evaluations before catalog changes;
- official MCP conformance for both protocol eras;
- an explicit production coverage denominator and behavior-specific ratchets;
- disjoint aggregate lanes;
- candidate-artifact and structured release simulations;
- deployment health/rollback policy; and
- performance history before timing thresholds.

The first goal is correctness and drift detection. Change-impact routing and performance gating follow measured history and may not weaken runtime diversity.

### 8. Keep runtime hardening with the adapters that own the state

Three audit clusters are real but should not become cross-cutting abstractions:

- **Node lifecycle module:** common startup/config/telemetry/shutdown policy around stdio/HTTP adapters, plus HTTP admission limits, idle expiry, initialization bounds, readiness, and cancellation on disconnect.
- **Worker request/auth module:** normalize request/origin/config once, keep raw-key and OAuth as distinct auth adapters, make OAuth the hosted default, remove per-request validation as an outage amplifier, and preserve metadata availability during Hevy outages.
- **CLI adapter modules:** co-locate route declaration, parsing, confirmation, and output while consuming operations, outcomes, and operator metadata.

Optional telemetry must never block serving, but exporter/provider implementations remain runtime-specific.

### 9. Simplify user-facing surfaces only after evidence exists

Tool/resource consolidation, canonical field migration, lazy resource links, bounded cache hints, and a read-only training-progress MCP App are product decisions downstream of the capability model and evaluation harness.

Do not reduce tool count to satisfy an advisory number. Retire or merge a surface only when task success, invalid/wasted calls, unsafe-action rate, token cost, and host support show a net gain. Structured content remains canonical; any MCP App stays an optional presentation adapter with text fallback.

## Dependency constraints for portfolio planning

These are hard ordering constraints, not the final implementation waves:

1. Generated-client closure can be repaired independently and should not wait for the architectural migration.
2. Invocation control/outcomes and the operations/capability seam precede adapter rewrites.
3. Protocol serving depends on a stable primitive/capability factory.
4. MCP/CLI contract projections depend on accepted operation descriptors and outcome shapes.
5. Operator diagnostics consume the outcome model and product metadata but can develop in parallel with repository topology.
6. Contract generation, AI evaluation, and conformance consume the models they enforce.
7. Surface removal and MCP Apps experimentation follow evaluation evidence.
8. Legacy removal follows a published compatibility policy and observed client/conformance support.

## Breaking-change ledger for the next decision

Likely **internal-only** changes:

- adding the operations workspace and moving policy out of core/CLI;
- replacing script registries and workflow composition with manifests;
- deleting shallow proxies, re-exports, unused interfaces, and superseded checkers;
- reorganizing Node lifecycle and Worker routing implementations.

Likely **additive or compatibility-preserving first**:

- cancellation/deadlines, phase-aware upstream errors, admission bounds;
- structured mutation and error fields alongside text;
- doctor/config inspection, readiness/version metadata;
- modern MCP metadata, conformance, resource links, and generated documentation.

Potentially **public-breaking and requiring an explicit migration budget**:

- `supersets_id` → `superset_id`;
- tool/resource consolidation or renamed public capabilities;
- CLI payload/config/error-envelope changes;
- moving raw Hevy keys out of standard `Authorization: Bearer` semantics;
- changing Node/CLI runtime requirements or executable command names; and
- eventually removing the 2025 protocol era.

No broad circuit breaker, indiscriminate stale user data, merged Node/Worker transport, credential elicitation, Tasks/sampling/roots adoption, universal progress, modern-only cutover, monolithic manifest, or timing threshold without history advances from synthesis.

## Disposition

The nine groups above are the deduplicated candidates for portfolio selection. The following are acceptance details inside those candidates, not standalone projects:

- safe-error projection and observation-lifecycle cleanup;
- response/pagination factory cleanup;
- shallow-module deletions;
- documentation drift checks;
- test-fixture consolidation;
- generated operation inventory cleanup; and
- workflow parser/helper extraction.

No implementation issue is created in this resolution. The remaining fog is now precise enough to graduate into two decisions:

1. set compatibility budgets, breaking-change eligibility, aliases/deprecation windows, and rollback guarantees per public surface;
2. select accepted/deferred/rejected candidates, implementation tiers and waves, dependencies, success measures, and the implementation-ready issue set.

Those decisions should remain sequential: portfolio selection depends on the compatibility budget.

  • MCP input/output schemas, annotations, structured mutation results, text compatibility, prompts/resources, titles/icons/completion metadata, and field mappings;
  • CLI route metadata, schema/examples/templates, JSON success/error envelopes, dry-run/replacement summaries, and command help; and
  • documentation and contract/evaluation fixtures.

CLI command modules remain local and domain-named because parsing and human presentation genuinely vary. MCP tools remain explicit capabilities rather than a generic stringly dispatcher. The shared descriptor removes duplicated knowledge without flattening either adapter.

4. Introduce one dual-era protocol-serving seam

One MCP primitive factory should serve both the 2025 interoperability floor and the 2026 opt-in protocol through SDK-supported adapters. It should own server/discover, per-request metadata, standard headers, cache hints, and legacy logging quarantine.

Node stdio, Node HTTP, and Worker HTTP remain separate adapters. Stateful Node session behavior stays isolated as legacy/runtime policy; Worker stateless request isolation stays intact. A modern-only cutover is not accepted without client and conformance evidence.

5. Build an executable operator experience contract

A structured product model should own surfaces, versions, Node requirements, auth modes, canonical endpoints, configuration schema/precedence, readiness states, diagnostics, upgrade/rollback, and recovery actions.

A deep doctor/preflight module should return versioned facts through human and JSON adapters, with ports for runtime, DNS/network, API auth, transport policy, OAuth metadata, and Worker bindings. README tables, package docs, deployment runbooks, migration indexes, and support bundles should be projections or validated examples, while hand-written prose retains rationale.

This consolidates operator diagnostics, safe failure facts, config normalization, hosted naming, readiness/version surfaces, deployment verification, and recovery guidance without making documentation a second registry.

6. Replace repository check duplication with linked control-plane models

Use separate but linked owners for:

  • topology: workspaces, dependency rules, exports, publishability, bundles, release propagation;
  • artifact provenance: spec normalization, generated destination, public barrels, manifests, packages/containers/Worker candidates; and
  • validation lanes: selector, runtime, credentials, artifacts, gate class, comparison semantics, and change-impact routing.

Local hooks, pull requests, release workflows, documentation, and drift jobs should consume these models. Runtime-diverse Vitest configurations and external GitHub/Cloudflare adapters remain separate.

The generated-client output defect is an independently actionable prerequisite: generation must target the tracked package tree, never recreate root src/, and a hermetic regenerate-and-clean-diff gate must prove closure before later safety-net work.

7. Generate enforcement and evidence from accepted models

The validation/evaluation layer should consume, not redefine, the capability, product, topology, and lane models. It owns:

  • complete tool/prompt/resource contract matrices;
  • deterministic AI-client task evaluations before catalog changes;
  • official MCP conformance for both protocol eras;
  • an explicit production coverage denominator and behavior-specific ratchets;
  • disjoint aggregate lanes;
  • candidate-artifact and structured release simulations;
  • deployment health/rollback policy; and
  • performance history before timing thresholds.

The first goal is correctness and drift detection. Change-impact routing and performance gating follow measured history and may not weaken runtime diversity.

8. Keep runtime hardening with the adapters that own the state

Three audit clusters are real but should not become cross-cutting abstractions:

  • Node lifecycle module: common startup/config/telemetry/shutdown policy around stdio/HTTP adapters, plus HTTP admission limits, idle expiry, initialization bounds, readiness, and cancellation on disconnect.
  • Worker request/auth module: normalize request/origin/config once, keep raw-key and OAuth as distinct auth adapters, make OAuth the hosted default, remove per-request validation as an outage amplifier, and preserve metadata availability during Hevy outages.
  • CLI adapter modules: co-locate route declaration, parsing, confirmation, and output while consuming operations, outcomes, and operator metadata.

Optional telemetry must never block serving, but exporter/provider implementations remain runtime-specific.

9. Simplify user-facing surfaces only after evidence exists

Tool/resource consolidation, canonical field migration, lazy resource links, bounded cache hints, and a read-only training-progress MCP App are product decisions downstream of the capability model and evaluation harness.

Do not reduce tool count to satisfy an advisory number. Retire or merge a surface only when task success, invalid/wasted calls, unsafe-action rate, token cost, and host support show a net gain. Structured content remains canonical; any MCP App stays an optional presentation adapter with text fallback.

Dependency constraints for portfolio planning

These are hard ordering constraints, not the final implementation waves:

  1. Generated-client closure can be repaired independently and should not wait for the architectural migration.
  2. Invocation control/outcomes and the operations/capability seam precede adapter rewrites.
  3. Protocol serving depends on a stable primitive/capability factory.
  4. MCP/CLI contract projections depend on accepted operation descriptors and outcome shapes.
  5. Operator diagnostics consume the outcome model and product metadata but can develop in parallel with repository topology.
  6. Contract generation, AI evaluation, and conformance consume the models they enforce.
  7. Surface removal and MCP Apps experimentation follow evaluation evidence.
  8. Legacy removal follows a published compatibility policy and observed client/conformance support.

Breaking-change ledger for the next decision

Likely internal-only changes:

  • adding the operations workspace and moving policy out of core/CLI;
  • replacing script registries and workflow composition with manifests;
  • deleting shallow proxies, re-exports, unused interfaces, and superseded checkers;
  • reorganizing Node lifecycle and Worker routing implementations.

Likely additive or compatibility-preserving first:

  • cancellation/deadlines, phase-aware upstream errors, admission bounds;
  • structured mutation and error fields alongside text;
  • doctor/config inspection, readiness/version metadata;
  • modern MCP metadata, conformance, resource links, and generated documentation.

Potentially public-breaking and requiring an explicit migration budget:

  • supersets_id → superset_id;
  • tool/resource consolidation or renamed public capabilities;
  • CLI payload/config/error-envelope changes;
  • moving raw Hevy keys out of standard Authorization: Bearer semantics;
  • changing Node/CLI runtime requirements or executable command names; and
  • eventually removing the 2025 protocol era.

No broad circuit breaker, indiscriminate stale user data, merged Node/Worker transport, credential elicitation, Tasks/sampling/roots adoption, universal progress, modern-only cutover, monolithic manifest, or timing threshold without history advances from synthesis.

Disposition

The nine groups above are the deduplicated candidates for portfolio selection. The following are acceptance details inside those candidates, not standalone projects:

  • safe-error projection and observation-lifecycle cleanup;
  • response/pagination factory cleanup;
  • shallow-module deletions;
  • documentation drift checks;
  • test-fixture consolidation;
  • generated operation inventory cleanup; and
  • workflow parser/helper extraction.

No implementation issue is created in this resolution. The remaining fog is now precise enough to graduate into two decisions:

  1. set compatibility budgets, breaking-change eligibility, aliases/deprecation windows, and rollback guarantees per public surface;
  2. select accepted/deferred/rejected candidates, implementation tiers and waves, dependencies, success measures, and the implementation-ready issue set.

Those decisions should remain sequential: portfolio selection depends on the compatibility budget.

Optional telemetry must never block serving, but exporter/provider implementations remain runtime-specific.

Tool/resource consolidation, canonical field migration, lazy resource links, bounded cache hints, and a read-only training-progress MCP App are product decisions downstream of the capability model and evaluation harness.

Do not reduce tool count to satisfy an advisory number. Retire or merge a surface only when task success, invalid/wasted calls, unsafe-action rate, token cost, and host support show a net gain. Structured content remains canonical; any MCP App stays an optional presentation adapter with text fallback.

Dependency constraints for portfolio planning

These are hard ordering constraints, not the final implementation waves:

  1. Generated-client closure can be repaired independently and should not wait for the architectural migration.
  2. Invocation control/outcomes and the operations/capability seam precede adapter rewrites.
  3. Protocol serving depends on a stable primitive/capability factory.
  4. MCP/CLI contract projections depend on accepted operation descriptors and outcome shapes.
  5. Operator diagnostics consume the outcome model and product metadata but can develop in parallel with repository topology.
  6. Contract generation, AI evaluation, and conformance consume the models they enforce.
  7. Surface removal and MCP Apps experimentation follow evaluation evidence.
  8. Legacy removal follows a published compatibility policy and observed client/conformance support.

Breaking-change ledger for the next decision

Likely internal-only changes:

  • adding the operations workspace and moving policy out of core/CLI;
  • replacing script registries and workflow composition with manifests;
  • deleting shallow proxies, re-exports, unused interfaces, and superseded checkers;
  • reorganizing Node lifecycle and Worker routing implementations.

Likely additive or compatibility-preserving first:

  • cancellation/deadlines, phase-aware upstream errors, admission bounds;
  • structured mutation and error fields alongside text;
  • doctor/config inspection, readiness/version metadata;
  • modern MCP metadata, conformance, resource links, and generated documentation.

Potentially public-breaking and requiring an explicit migration budget:

  • supersets_id → superset_id;
  • tool/resource consolidation or renamed public capabilities;
  • CLI payload/config/error-envelope changes;
  • moving raw Hevy keys out of standard Authorization: Bearer semantics;
  • changing Node/CLI runtime requirements or executable command names; and
  • eventually removing the 2025 protocol era.

No broad circuit breaker, indiscriminate stale user data, merged Node/Worker transport, credential elicitation, Tasks/sampling/roots adoption, universal progress, modern-only cutover, monolithic manifest, or timing threshold without history advances from synthesis.

Disposition

The nine groups above are the deduplicated candidates for portfolio selection. The following are acceptance details inside those candidates, not standalone projects:

  • safe-error projection and observation-lifecycle cleanup;
  • response/pagination factory cleanup;
  • shallow-module deletions;
  • documentation drift checks;
  • test-fixture consolidation;
  • generated operation inventory cleanup; and
  • workflow parser/helper extraction.

No implementation issue is created in this resolution. The remaining fog is now precise enough to graduate into two decisions:

  1. set compatibility budgets, breaking-change eligibility, aliases/deprecation windows, and rollback guarantees per public surface;
  2. select accepted/deferred/rejected candidates, implementation tiers and waves, dependencies, success measures, and the implementation-ready issue set.

Those decisions should remain sequential: portfolio selection depends on the compatibility budget.

## Question

Which synthesized opportunities should be accepted, deferred, or rejected; how should accepted work be tiered and sequenced; and what compatibility, deprecation, migration, and validation guarantees should govern breaking changes before separate implementation-ready issues are created?

## Wayfinder relationships

Parent map: [Chart a comprehensive hevy-mcp improvement roadmap](https://github.com/chrisdoc/hevy-mcp/issues/858)

- [Synthesize deep-module boundaries and cross-cutting opportunities](https://github.com/chrisdoc/hevy-mcp/issues/865)

comments.body:
## Resolution

This decision was completed through live human grilling after [Synthesize deep-module boundaries and cross-cutting opportunities](https://github.com/chrisdoc/hevy-mcp/issues/865#issuecomment-5166093667).

## Portfolio decision

Accept synthesis candidates 1–8 and the evidence-driven contract/surface simplification portion of candidate 9.

Defer the MCP Apps prototype until the canonical capability model and evaluation harness demonstrate enough user value and supported-host coverage. Do not create an implementation issue for it in this portfolio.

### Breaking-change policy

- Deliver one coordinated major release rather than spreading public breaks across several majors.
- Build it through small, independently mergeable pull requests on `main`.
- Preparatory work must preserve current public behavior through additive fields, compatibility adapters, or internal-only movement.
- Remove approved aliases and incompatible behavior only in the explicit final cutover.
- Internal package/script/workflow composition may break earlier when no public contract changes and repository validation remains green.

### Authentication policy

- Hosted production uses the existing MCP OAuth flow.
- Remove only the hosted raw-Hevy-key-as-`Authorization: Bearer` fallback in the coordinated major.
- Preserve direct Hevy credentials for Node, CLI, Docker, and self-hosted Worker operation.
- Preserve Hevy’s upstream `api-key` header; it is unrelated to the MCP OAuth bearer-token boundary.

### Protocol policy

Keep 2025 and 2026 MCP support throughout the entire next major. The 2026 protocol is too new for a modern-only cutover. Removing 2025 support requires:

1. a later major release;
2. passing official conformance for the modern path;
3. evidence from supported clients/hosts; and
4. a separately reviewed migration and rollback plan.

### Evidence gate for public surface consolidation

A tool/resource removal or merge may proceed only when recorded evaluations show:

- no task-success regression;
- zero unsafe-mutation regression;
- at least 15% improvement in median call count or catalog token cost; and
- confirmation across at least two supported AI client/model families.

Missing the threshold defers the consolidation without blocking the major release.

## Five-wave implementation backlog

Every issue below is unassigned and includes an ownership seam, bounded scope, non-goals, linked dependencies, migration policy, acceptance criteria, validation commands, and stopping conditions.

### Wave 1 — correctness closure

- [Repair generated-client output closure and enforce regeneration drift](https://github.com/chrisdoc/hevy-mcp/issues/870) — fix the current Kubb destination defect and add hermetic regenerate-and-clean-diff enforcement.

### Wave 2 — deep foundations

- [Establish end-to-end execution control and outcome semantics](https://github.com/chrisdoc/hevy-mcp/issues/871) — cancellation, absolute deadlines, phase-aware failures, retry safety, ambiguous writes, and shared recovery semantics.
- [Create the shared Hevy operations and capability workspace](https://github.com/chrisdoc/hevy-mcp/issues/872) — move shared MCP/CLI operation policy behind a runtime-neutral deep module.
- [Centralize repository topology, artifact provenance, and validation lanes](https://github.com/chrisdoc/hevy-mcp/issues/873) — replace duplicated package, artifact, release, and lane registries with linked control-plane models.

### Wave 3 — adapter projections and runtime policy

- [Project MCP contracts from canonical capability descriptors](https://github.com/chrisdoc/hevy-mcp/issues/874) — structured mutation results, canonical fields, schema semantics, pagination, and MCP presentation metadata.
- [Deepen the CLI adapter and add safe mutation ergonomics](https://github.com/chrisdoc/hevy-mcp/issues/875) — domain-local commands, stable JSON errors, schema discovery, previews, confirmation, completion, and complete reads.
- [Serve dual-era MCP protocols through one primitive factory](https://github.com/chrisdoc/hevy-mcp/issues/876) — SDK-supported 2025/2026 serving without duplicate primitive definitions.
- [Build the versioned operator contract and doctor interface](https://github.com/chrisdoc/hevy-mcp/issues/877) — product/config/auth/readiness semantics and privacy-safe diagnostics.
- [Consolidate Node lifecycle and bound HTTP session capacity](https://github.com/chrisdoc/hevy-mcp/issues/878) — shared Node startup/shutdown plus deterministic admission and cleanup.
- [Normalize Worker routing and make OAuth the hosted-only production path](https://github.com/chrisdoc/hevy-mcp/issues/879) — one request-normalization path, outage-aware validation, OAuth default, and staged hosted-fallback removal.

### Wave 4 — proof and enforcement

- [Generate the complete MCP contract matrix and conformance lane](https://github.com/chrisdoc/hevy-mcp/issues/880) — generated coverage for every primitive and both protocol eras.
- [Build task-based AI-client evaluations and decision evidence](https://github.com/chrisdoc/hevy-mcp/issues/881) — deterministic intent scenarios, optional two-family matrix, safety/call/token metrics, and base/head reports.
- [Apply one validation model to CI, artifacts, coverage, and releases](https://github.com/chrisdoc/hevy-mcp/issues/882) — disjoint lanes, honest coverage, exact candidate gates, release simulations, health, and rollback.
- [Generate operator documentation, status, and recovery projections](https://github.com/chrisdoc/hevy-mcp/issues/883) — synchronized consumer, deployment, migration, recovery, and teardown facts.

### Wave 5 — evidence-gated simplification and coordinated major cutover

- [Rationalize MCP discovery surfaces only when evaluation gates pass](https://github.com/chrisdoc/hevy-mcp/issues/884) — implement only consolidations that satisfy the agreed evidence threshold; closing with no removals is valid when they do not.
- [Execute the coordinated major public-contract cutover](https://github.com/chrisdoc/hevy-mcp/issues/885) — remove approved aliases and the hosted raw-key fallback, publish synchronized major artifacts, retain 2025 MCP, and verify the actual release/deployment plus rollback.

## Dependency and concurrency decision

The immediately takeable implementation frontier is:

- [Repair generated-client output closure and enforce regeneration drift](https://github.com/chrisdoc/hevy-mcp/issues/870)
- [Establish end-to-end execution control and outcome semantics](https://github.com/chrisdoc/hevy-mcp/issues/871)
- [Centralize repository topology, artifact provenance, and validation lanes](https://github.com/chrisdoc/hevy-mcp/issues/873)

These three may proceed in parallel because they own separate seams. All later bodies link their prerequisites explicitly. The final cutover depends on the entire accepted portfolio; an evidence-based no-op resolution of surface rationalization still satisfies that dependency.

## Global implementation contract

Every implementation issue must:

- start from a fresh worktree tracking current `origin/main`;
- preserve runtime-neutral package boundaries and never manually edit generated client output;
- identify the single owner/model it introduces or extends and the duplicate owners it deletes;
- use small conventional commits and include the Changeset required by repository policy;
- retain current public behavior until the final cutover unless the issue is explicitly additive;
- prove behavior through the module interface and replace superseded shallow tests rather than layering duplicate tests;
- run build, unit, style, type, changeset, and issue-specific validation;
- distinguish deterministic candidate proof from live external canaries;
- state what remains unverified; and
- stop before weakening security, privacy, compatibility, or a required gate.

No delivery is considered complete until the actual package, container, Worker, or release event and its downstream state are verified end to end.

## Deferred and rejected work

Deferred:

- MCP Apps prototype, pending capability/evaluation foundations and host evidence.
- Removal of 2025 MCP support, pending a later major and ecosystem evidence.
- Performance timing thresholds, pending stable history and variance data.

Not advancing:

- broad circuit breakers without production evidence;
- indiscriminate stale user data or OAuth validity;
- merged Node/Worker transport implementations;
- Tasks, sampling, roots, legacy SSE, or form elicitation for credentials;
- universal progress notifications;
- a monolithic repository/product/capability manifest; and
- tool-count reduction without task evidence.

## Completion

The accepted portfolio is fully represented by linked implementation-ready issues, its dependency frontier is visible, compatibility and rollback policies are explicit, and no planning fog remains. No source, test, configuration, documentation, generated, or deployment file was changed while resolving this ticket.

issue.title: Establish end-to-end execution control and outcome semantics
issue.body:
## Outcome

Every MCP, CLI, Node, and Worker invocation carries one cancellation signal and absolute deadline to Hevy, and every completion or failure produces a stable, privacy-safe outcome with retry and commit-state semantics.

## Ownership seam

A runtime-neutral execution/outcome module owns caller control, operation safety, request phase, commit state, safe failure taxonomy, and recovery fields. Adapters own only presentation and protocol/status mapping.

## Scope

- Add request control to every curated Hevy client operation and make fetch, body reads, backoff, pagination, and composite work abortable.
- Track dispatch/response phases and distinguish `not_sent`, `confirmed`, and `unknown` mutation outcomes.
- Select retryability from declared operation safety and remaining deadline; honor usable `Retry-After` values with jitter.
- Project the same safe outcomes into MCP structured errors, CLI exit/JSON errors, HTTP responses, and telemetry.
- Feed disconnect, eviction, SIGINT, and shutdown cancellation into active work.

## Non-goals

- Broad circuit breakers.
- Automatic retry of non-idempotent writes.
- Adapter-specific prose inside the shared model.
- Serving stale sensitive user data.

## Portfolio placement

Wave 2 — deep foundations

Primary priority: Resiliency

## Dependencies

- None. This issue is an immediate start within its wave.

## Migration and release policy

Land additively on main. Existing text remains available until the coordinated major cutover; new structured outcome fields may ship earlier as additive behavior. Include a runtime-visible Changeset.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Cancellation interrupts fetch, body consumption, backoff, pagination, and multi-source work.
- [ ] Total elapsed work stays inside one caller budget across all attempts.
- [ ] Non-idempotent writes are never automatically retried and uncertain writes report `safe_to_retry: false` plus unknown commit state.
- [ ] All adapters map the same taxonomy without leaking raw errors or credentials.
- [ ] Fault-injection tests cover cancellation, deadline, 429/Retry-After, network loss before/after dispatch, and forced shutdown.

## Validation

- `npm run build`
- `npx vitest run --exclude tests/integration/**`
- `npm run check`
- `npm run check:types`
- `npm run check:changeset`

## Stopping conditions

- Do not make a deadline reset per attempt or page.
- Stop if the design requires `hevy-client` to import an upper-layer MCP/CLI package; move shared low-level control types downward instead.

issue.title: Consolidate Node lifecycle and bound HTTP session capacity
issue.body:
## Outcome

Node stdio and HTTP share one startup/config/telemetry/shutdown lifecycle while HTTP sessions and initialization consume bounded, observable capacity.

## Ownership seam

The Node runtime owns process lifecycle, stdio/HTTP adapters, admission, session state, telemetry providers, and shutdown. Shared operation/outcome behavior stays below it.

## Scope

- Remove duplicated startup paths for config, telemetry, key validation, update checks, failure recording, and shutdown.
- Add session caps, idle expiry, initialization concurrency limits, application body deadlines, and deterministic cleanup.
- Return stable 429/503 recovery guidance for local capacity rejection.
- Cancel active upstream work on disconnect, eviction, and shutdown.
- Contain optional telemetry initialization/export failures so they cannot prevent serving.

## Non-goals

- Merging Node and Worker transports.
- Adding process restart supervision inside the library.
- Weakening host, bearer, body, or session security checks.
- Broad circuit breakers.

## Portfolio placement

Wave 3 — adapter projections and runtime policy

Primary priority: Resiliency

## Dependencies

- [Establish end-to-end execution control and outcome semantics](https://github.com/chrisdoc/hevy-mcp/issues/871)
- [Build the versioned operator contract and doctor interface](https://github.com/chrisdoc/hevy-mcp/issues/877)

## Migration and release policy

Preserve current stdio and HTTP invocation syntax until coordinated cutover. New capacity settings must have safe documented defaults and additive configuration first.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Common lifecycle behavior has one implementation across stdio and HTTP.
- [ ] Capacity, expiry, and initialization limits are deterministic and recover after eviction.
- [ ] Disconnect and shutdown abort active Hevy work within the configured bound.
- [ ] Optional telemetry failure cannot block startup, requests, or cleanup.
- [ ] Existing raw-chunk stdio instrumentation and HTTP security tests remain green.

## Validation

- `npm run test:stdio`
- `npm run test:contract`
- `npm run test:worker-http`
- `npm run build`
- `npx vitest run --exclude tests/integration/**`
- `npm run check`
- `npm run check:types`
- `npm run check:changeset`

## Stopping conditions

- Do not introduce unbounded queues behind the admission limit.
- Stop if common lifecycle extraction erases real stdio/HTTP differences.

issue.body:
## Outcome

Local, pull-request, release, and deployment workflows consume one validation-lane model, test every public candidate artifact, and enforce honest coverage/release semantics without duplicated execution.

## Ownership seam

Safety-net consumers own workflow orchestration, reporters, credentials, artifact gates, coverage aggregation, and release/deployment policy. Stable lane facts come from the repository control plane.

## Scope

- Make aggregate lanes disjoint while retaining focused debug commands and intentional runtime diversity.
- Define and baseline the production coverage denominator; merge reports deterministically and add behavior-specific ratchets.
- Gate Node and CLI tarballs, Docker image, and Worker candidate artifacts before publication/deployment.
- Add structured release simulations for Node-only, CLI-only, Worker-only, mixed, release-PR, and publish cases.
- Separate deterministic artifact gates from retried live canaries with explicit health, rollback, and manual-override policy.
- Record execution count and wall-time before and after without weakening correctness.

## Non-goals

- Inventing a global coverage percentage before measuring the denominator.
- Making transient Hevy availability block package publication.
- Removing SHA pinning or security scans.
- Change-impact optimization before lane parity.

issue.title: refactor: track architecture review findings across runtime and tooling
issue.body:
## Outcome

Turn the 2026-08-07 architecture review into owned implementation work without duplicating the existing roadmap. Each finding should either be routed to an existing issue, receive a focused successor issue, or be explicitly deferred with evidence.

The desired end state is less cross-module policy duplication, shorter validation feedback, deeper runtime-neutral operations, simpler runtime/test internals, and a more navigable repository control plane.

## Review baseline

- Repository snapshot: `origin/main` at `2443cad60f74c21ec38592d2083e7fac1398401a`.
- Exact local PR lane: `mise exec -- npm run test:pr -- --outputStyle=stream`.
- Cold run: **62.1s**; warm run: **33.0s**.
- The cold Nx report attributed **33.8s / 55%** to recoverable work; the warm report still attributed **13.8s / 43%**.
- `test:unit` selected 76 files / 842 tests. The contract, stdio, and CLI lanes added 13 file executions whose files were already selected by unit.
- The review was read-only: the source checkout and dedicated review worktree remained clean.

## Findings and current ownership

| # | Finding | Strength | Current owner / review delta |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | One runtime-neutral endpoint policy module | **Strong — top recommendation** | Adjacent to #928, but not owned there as a cross-runtime source for retry semantics, expected 404s, safe diagnostics, and metric endpoint identity. Keep #928 responsible for failure reporting and telemetry ownership. |
| 2 | Complete the shared Hevy operations module | **Strong** | Continue #872. The workspace currently shares `workouts.list`; Core and CLI still independently implement other pagination, read, mutation, search, and aggregation workflows. |
| 3 | Make PR validation artifact-aware and disjoint | **Strong** | Continue #882 with the measured baseline above. Unit overlaps focused lanes, and package/performance paths rebuild artifacts already produced earlier in the graph. |
| 4 | Collapse Node lifecycle into one runner | **Strong** | Continue #878. The stdio and HTTP paths still repeat process tracking, cancellation, config, run spans, update scheduling, shutdown, telemetry flush, and failure classification. |
| 5 | Deepen deterministic MCP test support | **Strong** | Reassess #606, which is closed as `not_planned`. The two mocked integration suites still repeat server/client/runtime registration, in-memory transport, network isolation, and teardown; Core tool tests also repeat registration/handler discovery. |
| 6 | Compile and partition response contracts | **Worth exploring** | No direct issue found; #874 is adjacent but owns public MCP contract projection, not this private implementation. `response-contracts.ts` is 1,252 lines, constructs a Zod object during each render, and repeats pagination mechanics. Benchmark before claiming material runtime gain. |
| 7 | Measure Worker request admission before caching | **Speculative** | Continue #879. Every Worker POST currently performs an upstream `/v1/user/info` validation and creates/connects a new server and transport. Add a repeated-request Worker benchmark before considering any bounded reuse. |
| 8 | Deepen the repository control plane | **Worth exploring** | #873 is complete and #882 is adjacent, but residual duplication remains across control-plane validation, lane rendering, Nx metadata, selectors, and handwritten docs. Current onboarding still says five workspaces instead of six and references deleted paths. |

## Evidence by finding

### 1. Endpoint policy duplication

Relevant files:

- `packages/hevy-client/src/hevy-client-kubb.ts`
- `packages/core/src/utils/hevy-error-policy.ts`
- `packages/core/src/utils/error-policy.ts`
- `packages/node/src/utils/hevy-client-observability.ts`
- `packages/operations/src/workouts.ts`

Endpoint identity and policy are represented by independent lists or branches. A change can therefore drift between client retry behavior, Core read-miss handling, safe diagnostics, operations behavior, and Node metric normalization.

The central model must keep distinct policy facts rather than flattening them into one broad allowlist. Unknown endpoints must remain fail-closed, and diagnostic redaction must not be weakened.

### 2. Shared operations remain shallow

Relevant files:

- `packages/operations/src/workouts.ts`
- `packages/operations/src/index.ts`
- `packages/core/src/tools/*.ts`
- `packages/cli/src/commands/index.ts`

The operations workspace proves the desired seam through `workouts.list`, but most Core tools and CLI commands still orchestrate the curated Hevy client separately. Grow #872 domain by domain; adapters should retain argument parsing, presentation, and runtime observation rather than Hevy-domain workflow policy.

### 3. Validation repeats tests and builds

Relevant files:

- `project.json`
- `nx.json`
- `package.json`
- `repository/validation-lanes.json`
- `tests/package/*`
- `.github/workflows/build-and-test.yml`

Specialized contract, stdio, and CLI tests are all selected by unit and then executed again by their named lanes. The build/pack path also rebuilds Node and CLI artifacts inside package smoke work after earlier graph producers have run.

Disjointness must preserve complete coverage and focused debugging commands. Artifact consumers must reject stale output; this is not permission to remove custom policy checks or package-install smoke behavior.

### 4. Node lifecycle duplication

Relevant files:

- `packages/node/src/index.ts`
- `packages/node/src/utils/graceful-shutdown.ts`
- `packages/node/src/streamable-http.ts`
- `packages/node/src/index.test.ts`

`runStdioServer` and the HTTP runner repeat one substantial lifecycle implementation. A private lifecycle runner with two real transport adapters would improve locality without erasing transport-specific behavior.

### 5. Repeated deterministic test machinery

Relevant files:

- `tests/integration/mocked/hevy-mcp.mocked.integration.test.ts`
- `tests/integration/mocked/get-workout-count-events-mocked.integration.test.ts`
- `packages/core/src/tools/*.test.ts`
- `docs/testing-strategy.md`

This is renewed current-state evidence for #606. A shared test-support module should remain private, fail on leaked sessions/interceptors/network calls, and preserve visible failure diagnostics.

### 6. Response-contract implementation breadth

Relevant files:

- `packages/core/src/utils/response-contracts.ts`
- `packages/core/src/utils/response-contracts.test.ts`

Keep the existing deep public response interface. Explore compiling each validation schema once and organizing private domain implementations around shared pagination behavior. Preserve exact structured schemas and legacy text output.

### 7. Unmeasured Worker admission cost

Relevant files:

- `packages/worker/src/worker.ts`
- `packages/worker/src/worker.test.ts`
- `tests/performance/scenario.ts`
- `tests/performance/performance.test.ts`

The first deliverable is a representative repeated-request benchmark. Any reuse design must explicitly preserve credential revocation, tenant isolation, request isolation, and stateless transport semantics.

### 8. Residual control-plane drift

Relevant files:

- `scripts/control-plane-validation.mjs`
- `scripts/control-plane-models.mjs`
- `scripts/repository-control-plane.mjs`
- `scripts/render-validation-lanes.mjs`
- `repository/validation-lanes.json`
- `project.json`
- `docs/contributor-onboarding.md`
- `docs/testing-strategy.md`

`control-plane-validation.mjs` is 1,091 lines. Twenty-six of 28 mapped lanes repeat the same alias and Nx target name. Validation/rendering code rereads overlapping sources, while handwritten changing facts have drifted.

Derive simple one-to-one projections from one validated model seam. Preserve custom commands, cache exceptions, runtime/package policy, release policy, and the compiler-backed dependency checker as explicit policy.

## Recommended routing order

1. Define the endpoint-policy ownership and coordinate it with #928.
2. Add the measured validation baseline and artifact-flow slice to #882.
3. Decide whether to reopen #606 or file a narrowed successor.
4. Continue shared operations through #872 and Node lifecycle through #878.
5. File a focused response-contract implementation/benchmark issue if accepted.
6. Add the Worker benchmark requirement to #879 before any reuse design.
7. Route residual control-plane and documentation drift to #882 or a focused successor.

This is an ordering for maintainer leverage, not a requirement to combine the work into one branch or pull request.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Every finding above is marked accepted, deferred, or rejected with a short rationale.
- [ ] Every accepted finding has exactly one owning issue; existing issues are reused where their scope already matches.
- [ ] The endpoint-policy owner distinguishes retry, expected-absence, diagnostic-safety, and metric-identity facts and remains fail-closed for unknown endpoints.
- [ ] #882 records the cold/warm baseline and requires before/after execution counts and wall time without weakening validation.
- [ ] #606 is either reopened, replaced by a narrower issue, or remains closed with a current rationale that addresses the repeated setup still present.
- [ ] Response-contract work is preceded by an allocation/render benchmark and preserves externally visible contracts.
- [ ] #879 receives a repeated-request Worker benchmark before any validation or server reuse is approved.
- [ ] Residual control-plane/docs drift has an owner and generated/parity-checked projections replace only derivable duplication.
- [ ] Accepted runtime/package changes identify their Changeset cascade from `repository/topology.json`.
- [ ] No accepted item requires editing `packages/hevy-client/src/generated/` by hand.

## Guardrails

- Preserve runtime-neutral direction: `hevy-client → operations → core`, with Node, Worker, and CLI as independent adapters.
- Keep generated client internals private and regenerated from their source.
- Keep npm scripts as compatibility entrypoints while Nx owns graph/input/output/cache metadata.
- Preserve the custom compiler-backed package-policy check; generic tooling may complement but not silently replace it.
- Do not broaden safe diagnostic data while deduplicating endpoint/error policy.
- Do not add Worker credential caching or shared mutable state without revocation and isolation evidence.
- Do not turn this tracking issue into one large implementation pull request.

## Validation expectations

Each implementation issue should run the focused lane for its changed seam plus the repository baseline:

```text
mise exec -- npm run check
mise exec -- npm run check:types
mise exec -- npm run build
mise exec -- npm run test:pr
mise exec -- npm run test:performance
mise exec -- npm run check:changeset
```

Performance-oriented work must publish the exact before/after command, cold/warm state, execution count, wall time, and any correctness trade-off.

## Non-goals

- Reopening completed roadmap issues merely to duplicate their accepted scope.
- Creating a second operations, lifecycle, Worker-routing, or validation model beside #872, #878, #879, or #882.
- Removing safety, release, package, privacy, or compatibility checks to improve timing.
- Designing a Worker cache before measuring the actual hot path.
- Splitting cohesive modules only because they are large.

## Review relationship

This is a current-checkout follow-up to the completed synthesis in #865 and portfolio decision in #866. It records what remains observable after subsequent architecture and Nx work, and routes those deltas into the live backlog.

One coordinated major release. Preparatory work lands incrementally on main with current behavior preserved; this issue is the explicit public cutover. Protocol removal requires a later evidence-backed major.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Every breaking change has an old-to-new mapping, automation-friendly diagnostic, and rollback path.
- [ ] All predecessor compatibility aliases are either deliberately removed or explicitly retained with rationale.
- [ ] Hosted production accepts MCP OAuth and rejects the retired raw-key bearer fallback; local/self-hosted direct keys still work.
- [ ] Both MCP protocol eras pass their accepted contract/conformance baselines.
- [ ] Exact candidate artifacts pass all release gates and the actual downstream release/deployment event is verified.

## Stopping conditions

- Do not release while any migration mapping, candidate artifact, conformance baseline, or rollback path is unverified.

issue.title: refactor: redesign observability with Sentry error reporting and OTel traces
issue.body:
## Problem Statement

The current observability system is present but not reliably actionable. Operators can see that an MCP session, tool, or process failed, but often cannot determine why, which release introduced the problem, which MCP client experienced it, or whether multiple events represent the same underlying failure.

The current design also spreads telemetry policy across the Node entrypoint, tool observer, SDK observer, API observer, core observation types, tests, and documentation. Each new diagnostic field requires more manual allowlisting and more privacy regression tests. That has created a choice between exporting opaque errors and exporting native exceptions with an unacceptable risk of leaking user data.

Issue #915 documented a concrete example: hundreds of process-failure traces were grouped under generic `McpProcessFailure`/`Error` fields without enough information to distinguish runtime, transport, SDK, and application failures. PR #920 explored moving more of the privacy decision into the Collector, but it changes the data policy before the desired observability contract and introduces raw exception plumbing into the runtime-neutral core.

The current error destination is a self-hosted GlitchTip project. We want to return to Sentry as the error-reporting backend, with proper release tracking, issue grouping, source maps, alerts, and trace correlation. GlitchTip should be removed from the active configuration and documentation.

### Goals

- Make user-visible failures actionable in Sentry.
- Make OTel traces explain what happened before and during a failure.
- Preserve low-cardinality metrics for reliability and performance dashboards.
- Capture sanitized exception messages and stacks without exporting prompts, tool arguments, tool results, credentials, or fitness data.
- Report each logical failure once instead of duplicating it across nested spans and SDK hooks.
- Keep the core package runtime-neutral and free of native exception transport concerns.
- Make the telemetry implementation easier to change by concentrating policy behind a small, deep Node adapter.
- Migrate error reporting from GlitchTip to Sentry SaaS without losing release/source-map diagnostics.

## Solution

Adopt a deliberate two-backend model:

- **Sentry** is the source of truth for actionable errors, crashes, releases, issue grouping, source maps, and error alerts.
- **OpenTelemetry through the Collector to Honeycomb** is the source of truth for traces, latency, retries, sessions, and aggregate metrics.
- **The Collector** performs tail sampling, routing, retention, and final defense-in-depth scrubbing. It is not the only privacy policy enforcement point.

Sentry performance tracing remains disabled. OTel traces remain independent from Sentry, with OTel trace and span identifiers attached to Sentry error events for navigation between systems.

### Failure reporter seam

Introduce one deep Node-only failure-reporting module with a small interface. Callers provide the native error and structured failure context; the module returns an optional correlation/event receipt.

The module will:

1. Classify known error types such as Hevy HTTP, network, validation, protocol, SDK, lifecycle, and process failures.
2. Produce one stable failure record containing bounded taxonomy and operational context.
3. Sanitize the message and stack once, with length, line, path, credential, URL, and nested-cause limits.
4. Send one sanitized exception to Sentry.
5. Attach the same structured fields and a standard exception event to the owning OTel span.
6. Link the Sentry event to the active OTel trace and expose a short diagnostic/correlation ID where appropriate.
7. Treat telemetry failures as best-effort and never alter MCP behavior.

The runtime-neutral core will retain only safe observation data. Native `unknown` exceptions will not be added to the core observation contract. The Node observer already wraps execution and can retain the native error at the Node seam.

### Approved diagnostic data

Capture as structured context:

- service, release, runtime, OS, and architecture;
- MCP transport and sanitized client/protocol metadata;
- fixed tool name, feature, operation, and read/write kind;
- API method, normalized endpoint, status, retry count, timeout phase, and commit state;
- stable error type, category, code, expectedness, and retryability;
- bounded sanitized message and stack for actionable failures;
- OTel trace/span IDs, Sentry event ID, and a per-failure diagnostic ID.

Never capture:

- API keys, bearer tokens, authorization headers, or request bodies;
- prompts, prompt arguments, tool arguments, or tool result text;
- raw Hevy identifiers, exact dates, workout/routine/template content, names, notes, or measurements;
- arbitrary error object properties, complete response bodies, or URLs containing query data;
- a persistent identity derived from the Hevy API key.

Telemetry is enabled by default for the packaged Node runtime. `HEVY_MCP_TELEMETRY=0` disables all project telemetry. Add a separate diagnostic-detail opt-out so users can retain structural metrics/traces while suppressing exception messages and stacks.

### Error ownership

Define one owner for each logical failure:

- Tool exceptions are captured by the Node tool observer.
- API observers supply structured API context; the tool-level reporter owns the user-visible exception.
- Returned MCP errors affect span status and metrics but do not create exception events.
- Expected not-found outcomes affect metrics and traces but do not create Sentry issues.
- SDK/protocol failures are captured by the SDK adapter.
- Startup and process failures are captured once by the lifecycle/process adapter.
- Telemetry exporter failures are not reported as application failures.

Nested spans may still receive status and bounded attributes, but the native exception is recorded only on the owning span.

### Sentry migration

Move the default error destination from GlitchTip to Sentry SaaS:

- Provision/configure the Sentry project, environments, ownership, retention, and alerts.
- Use a packaged public Sentry DSN with a runtime `SENTRY_DSN` override; an empty value disables Sentry export.
- Continue using the Sentry organization, project, and auth token in release CI for private source-map upload.
- Configure explicit Sentry integrations so automatic process handlers do not duplicate the custom failure reporter.
- Use `captureException` once per logical failure rather than generic exception messages for actionable errors.
- Add a centralized `beforeSend` final scrubber.
- Set release, environment, stable fingerprints, bounded tags/contexts, and OTel trace correlation.
- Generate source maps during release builds, upload them privately to Sentry, and keep them out of the published package.
- Remove active GlitchTip configuration, documentation, tests, and default DSN references. Historical changelog entries may remain as historical records.
- Audit and remove the direct Sentry OTel integration dependency if it is no longer needed after the independent OTel design is complete.

### OTel and Collector behavior

Keep OTel responsible for traces and metrics:

- Preserve a clear session/request → MCP tool → Hevy API → retry/cache span hierarchy.
- Use standard span status and exception semantics with the sanitized failure record.
- Keep messages and stacks out of metric attributes.
- Retain all error and slow traces at the Collector, and sample successful traces.
- Keep all low-cardinality metrics, with alerts for exporter drops, stale data, queue pressure, and Collector health.
- Maintain a final Collector scrubber and regression fixtures, but do not rely on the Collector as the sole privacy control.

### Worker alignment

The Worker must not import Node telemetry. After the Node design is proven, add a separate Worker adapter that emits the same failure taxonomy and correlation fields through the Worker’s supported logging/error facilities. A Worker-side OTel SDK is not part of the first implementation slice.

## Commits

Each commit below must leave the repository buildable and tests runnable. Runtime/package commits require the appropriate non-empty Changeset before committing, and the Changeset status check must pass before each commit that is prepared for review.

1. **`docs: define observability goals and data contract`**
   - Record the two-backend responsibility split, approved diagnostic fields, prohibited data, retention assumptions, and the Sentry migration decision.
   - Define the failure taxonomy, expected-error policy, and ownership matrix.

2. **`test: add representative failure and redaction fixtures`**
   - Add fixtures for Hevy HTTP errors, network errors, validation errors, SDK errors, process failures, malformed thrown values, nested causes, credentials, local paths, and response-body sentinels.
   - Establish tests against externally visible normalized records rather than private helper implementation details.

3. **`refactor: introduce the centralized failure record normalizer`**
   - Implement the single classifier/scrubber that produces bounded operational fields and sanitized diagnostic details.
   - Keep native error objects inside the Node package.
   - Verify stable behavior for expected errors and unknown thrown values.

4. **`refactor: add the Node failure reporter seam`**
   - Add the small reporter interface and adapters for Sentry and OTel.
   - Add correlation/event receipt handling.
   - Preserve best-effort behavior and make provider failures invisible to MCP callers.

5. **`refactor: route lifecycle and process failures through the reporter`**
   - Replace scattered lifecycle exception attribute construction with structured failure contexts.
   - Ensure startup, connect, runtime, uncaught-exception, and unhandled-rejection failures are captured once.
   - Preserve Node’s normal termination semantics.

6. **`refactor: route tool failures through one owner`**
   - Let the Node tool observer retain and report native tool exceptions at its execution seam.
   - Keep the core completion observation safe and runtime-neutral.
   - Stop the SDK wrapper and nested spans from emitting duplicate native exception events.

7. **`refactor: remove obsolete raw-exception plumbing and duplicated policy`**
   - Remove the proposed native exception field from the core observation contract if present.
   - Delete per-call privacy allowlist spreading and obsolete generic exception adapters.
   - Keep only one source of truth for failure context construction.

8. **`feat: restore Sentry SaaS as the error backend`**
   - Replace the GlitchTip default destination with the packaged Sentry DSN and runtime override behavior.
   - Configure explicit integrations, release/environment metadata, stable fingerprints, `beforeSend` scrubbing, and OTel trace correlation.
   - Update provider mocks and tests for one-event capture and duplicate-handler prevention.

9. **`build: upload private Sentry release artifacts`**
   - Make release builds generate and upload source maps to Sentry without including them in the npm package.
   - Add a release smoke test that verifies readable mapped stack frames and release attribution.

10. **`feat: align OTel span exception and sampling behavior`**
    - Record sanitized standard exception events only on owning spans.
    - Normalize span names and semantic attributes.
    - Add slow/error trace sampling rules and preserve all low-cardinality metrics.

11. **`chore: remove GlitchTip configuration and documentation`**
    - Remove active GlitchTip references, default DSN fixtures, destination assumptions, and obsolete environment descriptions.
    - Leave historical changelog records untouched.
    - Audit dependencies and remove direct packages that are no longer used.

12. **`feat: add observability dashboards and incident runbook`**
    - Migrate error views and alerts from GlitchTip to Sentry.
    - Add release, tool, client, API-status, startup, latency, and trace-correlation views.
    - Document the operator workflow from a Sentry issue to its Honeycomb trace.

13. **`test: verify end-to-end telemetry payloads`**
    - Exercise the actual Sentry event normalization hook and serialized OTel exporter payloads.
    - Verify secret/path/body/prompt absence, one-event ownership, release metadata, source-map attribution, Collector redaction, and exporter-failure resilience.

14. **`feat: align Worker failure diagnostics`**
    - Implement the same stable taxonomy and bounded correlation fields using Worker-supported facilities.
    - Keep this adapter independent from Node packages and defer Worker OTel SDK adoption unless a separate decision approves it.

15. **`refactor: remove superseded telemetry implementation`**
    - Delete dead helpers, stale tests, obsolete documentation, and compatibility paths only after the new behavior has been observed in a controlled release.

## Decision Document

- Sentry SaaS is the error-reporting backend. GlitchTip is removed from active runtime configuration.
- Honeycomb through the OTel Collector remains the trace and metric backend.
- Sentry performance tracing is disabled; OTel tracing is independent.
- Sentry receives one sanitized exception per logical actionable failure.
- OTel receives one sanitized exception event on the owning span plus structured span status/attributes.
- The Collector is a final safety and routing layer, not the only privacy enforcement layer.
- Error messages and stacks are allowed only after centralized bounded scrubbing.
- Prompts, arguments, results, credentials, raw IDs, exact dates, response bodies, and arbitrary object fields remain prohibited.
- No API-key-derived user hash or persistent user behavior identity is introduced.
- A per-failure diagnostic/correlation ID is preferred over persistent user tracking.
- The Node core interface remains runtime-neutral and does not transport native exceptions.
- Sentry’s automatic process-level handlers must not compete with the custom failure reporter.
- Expected not-found and ordinary user/configuration failures should not create noisy Sentry issues; they remain queryable through OTel metrics and traces.
- Public Sentry DSN configuration may be packaged; Sentry auth tokens and release credentials remain CI secrets.
- Source maps are uploaded privately to Sentry and excluded from the public package.
- The first implementation focuses on Node. Worker parity follows after the Node contract is validated.

## Testing Decisions

Good tests will verify externally visible telemetry behavior: what is sent, where it is sent, how it is grouped, whether it correlates to a trace, and whether MCP behavior remains unchanged. Tests should not assert incidental helper structure or the exact number of internal function calls unless that number is part of the duplicate-event contract.

Test coverage will include:

- deterministic normalization of each known error family;
- bounded messages, stacks, causes, paths, codes, statuses, and endpoints;
- removal of credentials, headers, prompts, arguments, results, bodies, and raw identifiers;
- expected-error suppression from Sentry;
- one logical failure producing one Sentry event and one owning OTel exception event;
- OTel trace/span ID and Sentry event ID correlation;
- explicit Sentry integration configuration and absence of duplicate process handlers;
- Sentry release/environment/fingerprint behavior;
- private source-map upload and mapped release stacks;
- actual serialized OTLP spans rather than only mocked `recordException` calls;
- Collector redaction and tail-sampling fixtures;
- provider/network failures not affecting MCP responses, process termination, or shutdown;
- telemetry opt-out and diagnostic-detail opt-out behavior;
- Node/Worker package boundary rules;
- dashboard query smoke checks and telemetry freshness.

Validation for the implementation will include the repository build, formatting/lint checks, type checks, unit tests, focused Node stdio observability tests, release-build tests, and the required Changeset status check.

## Out of Scope

- Exporting raw prompts, tool arguments, tool results, API keys, authorization headers, full request/response bodies, or raw fitness data.
- Adding persistent user-level behavior tracking or deriving a user identity from the Hevy API key.
- Migrating Honeycomb, ClickHouse, or the OTel Collector to another vendor.
- Enabling Sentry performance tracing or adding a Sentry span processor to the OTel provider.
- Adding a Worker-side OTel SDK in the initial Node migration.
- Changing MCP response contracts or exposing internal stack traces to MCP clients.
- Rewriting historical changelog entries that mention GlitchTip.
- Building a general-purpose logging framework.

## Further Notes

- This issue supersedes the narrow diagnostic approach in #915 and should be treated as the architectural follow-up to PR #920.
- Before implementation begins, operators should inspect a representative sample of current Sentry/GlitchTip events and OTel traces, including the 578 process failures referenced by #915, to establish a baseline for noise, duplication, and missing context.
- Success means an operator can open a Sentry issue and answer: which release failed, which MCP client and tool were involved, what stable error/API condition occurred, whether the issue is new or regressed, and which Honeycomb trace shows the failure path.
- The migration should be released in a controlled canary first. Compare event volume, duplicate rate, mapped-stack coverage, trace correlation, and sensitive-field regression results before removing the old compatibility paths.

## Outcome

One primitive/capability factory serves the 2025 interoperability floor and the 2026 protocol through SDK-supported handlers across Node and Worker without duplicate tool definitions.

## Ownership seam

The protocol-serving module owns protocol-era negotiation, discovery/metadata, standard headers, cache hints, and legacy logging quarantine. Node stdio, Node HTTP, and Worker HTTP remain concrete adapters.

## Scope

- Adopt the SDK modern handler/factory for 2026 requests with documented 2025 fallback.
- Support modern discovery, per-request metadata, standard `Mcp-Method`/`Mcp-Name` headers, and cache hints.
- Keep stateful Node HTTP legacy behavior isolated from stateless Worker requests.
- Use the current SDK stdio serving path without losing required raw-chunk observability.
- Confine deprecated MCP logging to the legacy adapter.

## Non-goals

- Removing 2025 support in the next major.
- Merging Node and Worker transport implementations.
- Adopting Tasks, sampling, roots, legacy SSE, or universal progress.
- Reimplementing SDK protocol logic.

## Portfolio placement

Wave 3 — adapter projections and runtime policy

Primary priority: Resiliency and interoperability

## Dependencies

- [Create the shared Hevy operations and capability workspace](https://github.com/chrisdoc/hevy-mcp/issues/872)
- [Project MCP contracts from canonical capability descriptors](https://github.com/chrisdoc/hevy-mcp/issues/874)

Dual-era support is mandatory throughout the next major because the 2026 protocol is new. Removal may occur only in a later major after conformance and supported-client evidence.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The same primitive registry serves both protocol eras.
